title: Al-Humazah: the slanderer
hookLine: woe to the backbiter who counts his money and thinks it will keep him (Surah 104)

cards: He turns up at work, at school, at family dinners. The one doing impressions of a coworker the moment she leaves the room. The eye-roll across the table.
The group-chat screenshot with a laughing emoji. It feels small, and it feels safe, especially when you have more money, more status, more followers.
Today's surah has a word for this person, and it doesn't treat it as small at all. Nine lines, and it opens with woe.

teach.h: HUMAZAH, LUMAZAH — THE LOOK, THE TONGUE.
teach.b: Surah one hundred four begins, in Pickthall's translation: Woe unto every slandering traducer, Who hath gathered wealth of this world and arrangeth it. He thinketh that his wealth will render him immortal.
In Arabic the first line is two sharp words: humazah, lumazah. Commentators give them related shades. One mocks with gestures: the look, the smirk, the pointed finger.
The other wounds with the tongue, especially behind someone's back. Both make someone smaller so you can feel bigger.
Then the surah moves straight from mockery to money. The mocker is also the man counting his wealth, over and over, arranging it.
In the surah's picture, contempt for people and trust in money come from the same place: the belief that you're safe, above it all, untouchable.

teach.h: HE THINKS HIS WEALTH WILL KEEP HIM.
teach.b: He thinks his wealth will make him last forever. The surah says no, and describes a fire that reaches the heart, where the contempt began.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave a plain definition of backbiting, recorded in Sahih Muslim. He asked his companions: do you know what backbiting is? It's mentioning your brother in a way he would dislike.
Someone asked: what if it's true?

teach.h: EVEN IF IT'S TRUE, IT'S BACKBITING.
teach.b: He said: if it's true, that's backbiting. If it's false, that's slander. So the test isn't whether the joke is accurate.
It's whether they'd be hurt to hear it.
Money won't keep you. Neither will the laugh at someone else's expense.

how: Muslims recite al-Humazah in the prayers, and Islamic teaching treats backbiting (ghibah) and slander as serious wrongs; many try to leave a gathering or change the subject when others are mocked.

o: a boaster who brags about his wealth
one who mocks and belittles people
a traveler who wanders from town to town

games.q: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.
p: mocking by look and by tongue
thinks it will make him last
true, but he'd dislike hearing it

s: if what you say about someone is true, it isn't backbiting
the Prophet said: if it's true, that's backbiting. if false, that's slander.
the surah links mocking people with trusting in money
the mocker is the one counting his wealth, thinking it will keep him.

games.q: the Prophet defines backbiting: mentioning your brother in a way he'd dislike. someone asks, but what if it's true?
o: then it's backbiting; if false, it's slander
then say it to his face first
games.why: truth doesn't excuse it. the test is whether he'd be hurt to hear it (Sahih Muslim).

practice: Think honestly about the last time you mocked someone, out loud, in a message, or just with a look. No guilt; just see it clearly, and ask what you were protecting.
Then picture that person hearing it, and let the picture be real for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Al-Humazah. The slanderer, the one who mocks and belittles; the name of Surah one hundred four. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: one who mocks and belittles, the first key word of Surah 104.

carryVoice: Your line: money won't keep you. A joke that's true can still be backbiting. One hundred seventy days now.

sources.q: Woe unto every slandering traducer, Who hath gathered wealth (of this world) and arrangeth it. He thinketh that his wealth will render him immortal.

sources.ref: Qur'an 104:4–9 (the crushing fire that reaches the hearts)
